entries.meaning: Seated there without hesitation, Kaikeyī spoke bitter words whose severity could distress severity itself. Her tongue was a bow and her many words arrows, while the gentle king seemed their target; it was as though cruelty had assumed a body and, as a master warrior, was teaching archery. She related the whole affair to Rāma, sitting like mercilessness embodied. Rāma—the sun of the solar dynasty and the innate treasury of joy—smiled within and answered in flawless words, tender and lovely like ornaments of speech: ‘Listen, Mother: blessed indeed is the son who lovingly obeys his father and mother. A son who brings contentment to his parents is rare in all the world. Meeting the sages, especially in the forest, will benefit me in every way; and there I have my father’s command as well as your approval, Mother.’

‘Bharata, dear as life to me, will obtain the kingdom, while providence has today become favorable to me in every way. If I did not go to the forest for such a purpose, I should be counted foremost in an assembly of fools. Those who abandon the wish-fulfilling tree to tend the castor plant, or reject nectar and ask for poison, would not fail to seize an opportunity like this; consider it in your heart, Mother. Yet I have one particular sorrow: I see the king utterly distraught. I cannot believe that so slight a matter should cause Father such heavy grief. The king is steadfast, a fathomless ocean of virtues; perhaps I have committed some grave offense against him, on account of which he says nothing to me. By my oath, tell me the truth.’ Raghubar’s words were innately straightforward, but the malicious, crooked-minded woman construed them crookedly: a leech moves crookedly through water even though the water is uniform.

The queen was relieved when she perceived Rāma’s disposition, and spoke while displaying counterfeit affection: ‘By your oath and Bharata’s adjuration, I know of no other cause. Dear son, you are fit for no blame; mother, father, and kindred are givers of happiness. Rāma, everything you say is true, and you are devoted to the word of father and mother. Please reassure your father and say the same to him, so that no disgrace attaches to him in the fourth stage of life. It is improper to show disrespect to one whom merit has given a son like you.’ How could auspicious words issue from an inauspicious mouth? They were like sacred places such as Gayā situated in Magadha. All the mother’s words pleased Rāma, just as water that has entered the heavenly Gaṅgā becomes lovely. Remembering Rāma, the king emerged from his swoon and turned upon his side. The minister announced Rāma’s arrival and made the entreaty appropriate to that moment.

words: in the fourth stage of life

entries.meaning: When the king heard Rāma’s footfall, he summoned his fortitude and opened his eyes. The minister supported the king and seated him; as Rāma fell at his feet, the king gazed upon him. Overcome with affection, he took Rāma and clasped him to his breast, like a serpent recovering its lost jewel. The monarch remained looking at Rāma while streams of water flowed from his eyes. Overpowered by grief, he could say nothing and pressed Rāma to his heart again and again. Within his mind the king entreated providence to keep Raghunātha from going to the forest. Remembering Maheśa, he implored him: ‘Hear my prayer, eternal Śiva. You are quickly pleased, an unstinting giver; knowing me to be a suffering, helpless person, remove my distress. You impel the hearts of all: give Rāma such an intention that he will abandon my command and remain at home, setting aside his own noble nature and affection.’

‘Let me incur infamy and let my good name in the world perish; let me fall into hell rather than go to heaven. Make me endure every unbearable sorrow, but do not let Rāma pass beyond the shelter of my eyes.’ The king pondered thus without speaking, his mind trembling like a peepal leaf. Raghupati understood that his father was helpless under love and surmised that his mother might say something further. Suiting place, time, and occasion, he thoughtfully spoke these courteous words: ‘Father, I will say something that may be audacious; recognizing it as childishness, please forgive what is improper. You have suffered grief over a very small matter—why did no one tell me of it first? Seeing my lord in this state, I questioned Mother; on hearing the matter, my body became calm. This is an auspicious hour; Father, please relinquish anxiety born of affection. Glad at heart, give me your command.’ As the Lord said this, his limbs thrilled.

Blessed upon the earth is the birth of one whose conduct, when heard, delights his father. The four aims of life lie in the palm of one to whom father and mother are as dear as life. By obeying your command I shall obtain the fruit of birth; I shall return very quickly—only let me have your leave. I shall go ask leave of Mother and then depart for the forest after bowing again at your feet.’ Having said this, Rāma departed; the king, overwhelmed by grief, gave no answer. The exceedingly sharp news spread through the city and, upon touching people, seemed like a scorpion climbing over every body. Hearing it, all the men and women became distraught, like vines and trees at the sight of a forest blaze. Wherever anyone heard it, that person beat their head; grief was immense and composure could not remain. Mouths dried, eyes streamed, and grief would not fit within the heart—as though an army of the sentiment of pathos had sounded its advance and descended upon Ayodhyā.

At the very point of fulfillment, fate had spoiled the affair; everywhere people abused Kaikeyī: ‘What has come over this sinful woman? She has roofed the house only to set it on fire. She wishes to gouge out her own eyes with her own hands and then see; throwing away nectar, she wants to taste poison. Crooked, hard, foolish, and unfortunate, she has become to the Raghu lineage what fire is to a bamboo forest. Seated upon a branch, she has cut down its tree; amid happiness she has marshaled an array of grief. Rāma was always as dear as life to her—what cause made her resolve upon this crookedness?’ The poet says that a woman’s nature is truly inaccessible, fathomless, and concealed in every way; one might sooner grasp one’s own reflection, brother, than comprehend a woman’s course. What can fire not burn? What can the ocean not contain? What can a woman—called weak yet powerful—not do? Whom in this world does Time not devour?

‘Whom does fate wish to make hear what, and what has it made heard? Whom does it wish to show what, and what has it shown?’ Some said, ‘The king did not act well: without deliberation he granted boons to the malicious woman. By his obstinacy he has become the vessel of every grief; helpless before a woman, he seems to have lost wisdom and virtue.’ Others, recognizing the supreme limit of dharma, were prudent and did not blame the king; one person after another recounted the stories of Śibi, Dadhīci, and Hariścandra. Some alleged Bharata’s consent, while others listened and remained indifferent. Still others covered their ears, seized their tongue between their teeth, and said, ‘This charge is false. Your merit departs when you speak so: Rāma is dearer than life to Bharata. The moon may shed sparks of fire and nectar may become equal to poison, but Bharata would never, even in a dream, do anything hostile to Rāma.’

Some blamed the Creator, who had shown them nectar only to give them poison. The city was in turmoil; everyone was anxious, unbearable anguish burned in their hearts, and all enthusiasm had vanished. Brahmin women, senior women honored by their families, and those especially dear to Kaikeyī began advising her and praising her former good character, though their words struck her like arrows: ‘You have always said, “Bharata is not as dear to me as Rāma”; the whole world knows this. You naturally love Rāma—for what offense do you send him to the forest today? You never showed jealousy toward your co-wife; the entire land knows your affection and trust. What harm has Kauśalyā done now, on whose account you have hurled a thunderbolt upon the city? Will Sītā abandon her beloved’s company? Will Lakṣmaṇa remain at home? Will Bharata enjoy the kingdom in the capital? Will the king live without Rāma?’

‘Reflect thus and relinquish the anger in your heart; do not become a storehouse of sorrow and disgrace. By all means have Bharata made crown prince—but what business does Rāma have in the forest? Rāma is not hungry for kingship: he is a pillar of dharma and averse to the savor of sense objects. If separation is what you seek, let Rāma leave the palace and reside at his teacher’s house; obtain some other such boon from the king. If you do not heed what we say, nothing at all will come into your hands. If this was some jest you made, then say so and reveal it openly. Hearing that a son like Rāma was deemed fit for the forest, what will people say of you? Rise quickly and devise the very means by which sorrow and disgrace may be destroyed.’
